newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels win battle for Lubumbashi, take airport.
newsitem.headline: Rebels win battle for Lubumbashi, take airport.

text.p: Rebels took Lubumbashi airport on Thursday, winning the battle for Zaire's second city and making them lords of its economic heartland.
In a 90-minute gunfight, they sent the local remnants of President Mobutu Sese Seko's army running into the maize fields and bush around the airfield, some still armed, witnesses said.
"It was terrifying, I can't put my fear into words," said Marie-Josephine, who huddled with others in a hangar through the fighting, in which her soldier husband changed sides.
"Then the DSP (presidential guards) ran off. There were about 250 of them. I don't think many people were killed."

The rout of the hated DSP ended the battle for the capital of Shaba province, whose mineral wealth helped fund three decades of Mobutu rule until greed, corruption and political chaos crippled the copper and cobalt mines.

Casualties seemed low in the fight for control of the city. Missionaries said three rebel soldiers had been buried in a main cemetery. Hospitals reported only a handful of injured, including a Belgian recovering from shrapnel wounds.
Doctors, however, said the mortuary had received the bodies of seven civilians, whom they were told the rebels had shot for looting despite warnings not to.

Laurent Kabila's forces, welcomed as heroes and liberators in a wave of joy, slowly restored order in the city but not before looters stripped military bases and houses of Mobutu officials of everything, including the kitchen sinks.
"This is not looting, this is taking back what they stole from us for so long," one man said.
Abandoned weapons and ammunition were carted off from Mobutu's own villa, used as a DSP base, into a city now awash with arms.
White flags and headbands, signs of support for Kabila, covered the city. Symbols of the 32-year Mobutu era that has now ended here were swiftly and angrily eradicated.

People hauled down a statue of a hand carrying a flame, the symbol of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement (MPR) movement, scrawling "Mobutu is dead" on the bottom of the pedestal that lay in the road.
"Kabila is the new strong man of the Congo", read one slogan on a party monument, reverting to the old name of Zaire which the rebel Alliance favours.
Portraits of Mobutu in his trademark leopardskin hat, once obligatory in offices, were torn up.
The battle for Lubumbashi had begun in earnest early on Wednesday when rebels marched in, to cheers of adulation from civilians but short-lived street resistance from the DSP.

The rest of the regular soldiers changed sides or changed clothes, dumping uniforms and melting into the million-strong population. A plane flew out military top brass in the night, but left the rest of the DSP stranded and encircled.

Turncoat officers urged their former comrades in arms in Kinshasa to give up the fight. "We saw we were defending a lost cause. I appeal to the military in Kinshasa especially, put down your arms, let the liberation take place in peace," said Colonel Nsau Nzuzi of the Zairean army's 21st Infantry Brigade.

In just six months Kabila has wrested control of all of east Zaire, from the Ugandan border in the north to the Zambian and Angolan borders in the south. His domain covers about half the central African country, which is the size of Western Europe.
It includes all major cities bar the capital Kinshasa, and the economic the diamond mines of Kasai province, copper mines of Shaba, and gold mines of Kivu.
